references.text: The parallel text in Matthew where Jesus asks the crowd the same question after John's disciples have left: "What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?"
The continuation of the parallel in Matthew, where Jesus further asks the crowd what they went out to see—a man dressed in fine clothes, or a prophet.

The immediate context: John's disciples came to Jesus with the question of whether he was the one who was to come, and Jesus answered them by pointing to his deeds. Verse 24 introduces Jesus' speech to the crowd after these messengers had left.
The direct continuation where Jesus describes John as more than a prophet and identifies him as the messenger spoken of in Scripture, declaring that no one born of women is greater than John.
John grew up and was in the wilderness until the day he appeared before Israel—this explains why Jesus asks what the people went out into the wilderness to see.
John the Baptist appeared and preached in the wilderness of Judea, which forms the background for Jesus' question about what the people went out into the wilderness to see.

Paul urges believers not to be like children tossed here and there by waves and carried along by every wind of teaching—the image of a reed shaken by the wind is used by Jesus to contrast John's steadfastness.
The image of a reed swaying in water is used as a metaphor for instability. Jesus uses a similar image of a reed in the wind to emphasize that John was not an wavering or weak person.

John's ministry in the wilderness by the Jordan, where he preached a baptism of repentance. This is the background for Jesus' rhetorical question about what the people went out into the wilderness to see.
